claim_verdicts.bullet: Exact k-NN search requires O(N * D) distance computations per query, where N is the dataset size and D the dimensionality
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Exact k-NN search using exhaustive search requires O(N * D) complexity, thus is computationally inefficient as the data size becomes million or billion-scale, making exact k-NN search impractical to implement in real-time systems.

claim_verdicts.slide: Why Exact k-NN Doesn't Scale

claim_verdicts.slide: ANN Index Families — HNSW, IVF-PQ, DiskANN
claim_verdicts.bullet: HNSW recall is tuned via efSearch: increasing it from 100 to 500 raises recall from ~85% to ~98% but increases per-query latency from ~1 ms to ~5 ms on a 10 M-vector dataset
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: A higher efSearch (e.g., 500 vs. 100) increases recall by exploring more neighbors, but it slows down queries due to additional distance calculations. In a 10-million-vector dataset, efSearch=500 might achieve 98% recall but take 5ms per query, while efSearch=100 might drop to 85% recall with 1ms latency.

claim_verdicts.slide: ANN Index Families — HNSW, IVF-PQ, DiskANN
claim_verdicts.bullet: IVF-PQ combines cluster-based partitioning with product quantization; sweeping nprobe from 1 to 256 moves recall from ~70% to ~99% while throughput drops from 50,000 QPS to 300 QPS
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: With nprobe values ranging from 1 to 256, recall ranges from 70% to 99%, with query throughput decreasing from 50,000 QPS to 300 QPS and latency increasing from 0.02ms to 3.3ms respectively.

claim_verdicts.slide: ANN Index Families — HNSW, IVF-PQ, DiskANN
claim_verdicts.bullet: DiskANN stores the graph index on SSD with a compressed representation in RAM, enabling billion-point search on a single node with 64 GB RAM — achieving >5,000 QPS at 95%+ recall with <3 ms mean latency
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: On the billion point SIFT1B bigann dataset, DiskANN serves > 5000 queries a second with < 3ms mean latency and 95%+ 1-recall@1 on a 16 core machine with 64GB RAM and an SSD.

claim_verdicts.slide: Metadata Filtering, Consistency, and Silent Recall Loss
claim_verdicts.bullet: Metadata filtering interacts destructively with ANN graph traversal
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Naive pre-filtering achieves much lower recall than post-filtering, with maximum recall plateauing at ~57% compared to >99% for post-filtering. Non-matching nodes are not only poor result candidates, but also routing states that connect the search to other regions of the graph. Skipping their expansion prevents the search from reaching their neighbors, even when those neighbors match the predicate.

claim_verdicts.slide: RAG as a Two-Stage Data Pipeline
claim_verdicts.bullet: Chunking strategy is a foundational design decision: chunk size, overlap, and segmentation method define retrieval quality, and a well-tuned strategy can improve retrieval accuracy by up to 40% compared to naive approaches
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: In production LLM RAG pipelines, chunking is not just a preprocessing step — it defines the quality of retrieval and the effectiveness of agent memory. A well-tuned chunking strategy can improve retrieval accuracy by 40% compared to naive approaches.

claim_verdicts.slide: RAG as a Two-Stage Data Pipeline
claim_verdicts.bullet: Hybrid retrieval runs sparse BM25 and dense ANN search in parallel, then fuses the two ranked lists — ensuring lexical matches the dense model ranks too low (error codes, IP addresses, config flags) are not lost
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: In real systems that handle logs, docs, and configuration snippets, vectors alone regularly return answers that sound plausible but are wrong because they miss short, literal tokens like IPs, error codes, and config flags.

claim_verdicts.slide: Hybrid Search, RRF, and Re-Ranking
claim_verdicts.bullet: **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)** combines ranked lists by scoring each document *d* as RRFscore(*d*) = ∑ 1/(*k* + rank(*d*)), where *k* is typically 60; it requires no score normalisation and outperforms both Condorcet Fuse and individual rank-learning methods
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Reciprocal Rank Fusion is a simple method for combining the document rankings from multiple IR systems. RRF consistently yields better results than any individual system, and better results than the standard method Condorcet Fuse. The RRF formula scores each document d as: RRFscore(d) = sum over all ranking lists R of 1/(k + r_R(d)), where r_R(d) is the rank of document d in list R and k is a constant (typically 60). The method requires no score normalisation, operating purely on rank positions.
claim_verdicts.issue: The bullet says RRF 'outperforms both Condorcet Fuse and individual rank-learning methods'. The source says RRF yields 'better results than any individual system, and better results than the standard method Condorcet Fuse.' The source does not mention 'individual rank-learning methods' -- it says 'individual system' (meaning individual IR systems in the ensemble, not rank-learning methods). The bullet conflates 'individual system' with 'individual rank-learning methods', which are different concepts.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)** combines ranked lists by scoring each document *d* as RRFscore(*d*) = ∑ 1/(*k* + rank(*d*)), where *k* is typically 60; it requires no score normalisation and outperforms both Condorcet Fuse and any individual retrieval system in the ensemble [claim:agentic-de:045]

claim_verdicts.slide: Hybrid Search, RRF, and Re-Ranking
claim_verdicts.bullet: **Cross-encoder re-ranking** is the second stage: a bi-encoder retrieves 50-100 candidates quickly, then a cross-encoder jointly encodes each (query, document) pair to produce a refined relevance score, reordering candidates so the top 5-10 passed to the LLM are the most relevant
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Two-Stage (Bi-Encoder + Cross-Encoder): Query -> Embed -> Vector Search -> Top-100 -> Cross-Encoder Rerank -> Top-10 -> LLM. The study identified optimal hyperparameters: Retrieve 50-100 candidates, rerank to 10 documents, with batch size of 32 for optimal GPU performance.

claim_verdicts.slide: Hybrid Search, RRF, and Re-Ranking
claim_verdicts.bullet: **Recall vs. precision separation**: hybrid search improves recall (surfaces lexical matches the dense model misses), while re-ranking improves precision (reorders the already-retrieved set); a re-ranker cannot fix recall because it never sees documents that were not retrieved in the first stage
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Two-stage retrieval separates candidate generation (fast, broad search) from ranking (slow, precise evaluation). Your initial retrieval needs to be fast and cast a wide net. Your reranker needs to be accurate and selective. Cross-encoders process query and document together, capturing interactions between them for more accurate relevance scoring.

claim_verdicts.slide: The Top-k Cutoff Failure Mode
claim_verdicts.bullet: A canonical RAG failure occurs when a relevant chunk is retrieved but ranked just outside the top-k cutoff (e.g., at position 11 when k = 10) — the system indexed and retrieved the document, but the LLM never sees it, upper-bounding generation quality by the missing evidence regardless of the model's reasoning capacity
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Whenever a truly relevant document has rank greater than k, the model's generation is upper-bounded by missing evidence, regardless of reasoning capacity. When a document needed sits at position eleven in the results just outside the top ten, the system had not failed to index or retrieve it but it was ranked below ten other documents.
